shortest-path.name: Shortest path
shortest-path.tagline: Find the cheapest route between two nodes.
rules: You start on node A and must reach the target shown above the board.
Click a neighbouring node to move along an edge: its weight is added to your cost.
Use Undo to step back. When you reach the target, submit.
You win if your total cost equals the minimum possible.
theory: Dijkstra's algorithm (1956) solves this exactly. It keeps a tentative distance for every node and repeatedly settles the closest unsettled node, relaxing the edges that leave it.
It is greedy, and greed works here because weights are never negative: once a node is the closest unsettled one, no later detour can make it cheaper.
With a priority queue it runs in O((V + E) log V). It powers route planners and network routing protocols such as OSPF.

mst.name: Minimum spanning tree
mst.tagline: Connect every node using the lightest set of edges.
rules: Click an edge to select it, click again to deselect it.
Pick exactly n − 1 edges (the counter shows how many) that connect every node without forming a cycle.
You win if the total weight is the minimum possible. When several trees tie, any of them counts.
theory: A spanning tree reaches every node with no cycles; a graph with n nodes always needs exactly n − 1 edges for it.

Kruskal's algorithm sorts the edges by weight and adds each one unless it would close a cycle (checked with a union–find structure). Prim's algorithm grows one tree from a single node, always taking the cheapest edge that leaves it.

Both are correct thanks to the cut property: for any split of the nodes into two groups, the lightest edge crossing the split belongs to some minimum spanning tree. It is the classic model for building the cheapest network of cables, pipes or roads.
mst.lostDetail: Your tree weighs {weight} · minimum {best}. Green edges show an optimal tree.
mst.notTree: These edges are not a tree (there is a cycle or a node is left out). Minimum weight: {best}.

coloring.name: Graph colouring
coloring.tagline: Colour the nodes so neighbours never match, with as few colours as possible.
rules: Click a node to colour it; click again to switch colour (after the last one it goes back to blank).
Two nodes joined by an edge must have different colours: conflicting edges turn red.
Colour every node, then submit. You win with no conflicts and the minimum number of colours.
theory: The minimum number of colours needed is the chromatic number χ(G). A graph with χ ≤ 2 is bipartite: it has no cycle of odd length.
Deciding whether χ ≤ 3 is NP-complete, so no fast algorithm is known for big graphs. With a handful of nodes, trying every possibility (backtracking) is fine, and that is how this game checks you.

The four colour theorem (1976, one of the first computer-assisted proofs) says every planar map needs at most 4 colours. Colouring models scheduling too: exams that share students cannot go in the same slot.
coloring.wonDetail: {used} colours: that is the chromatic number.
coloring.conflictDetail: {count, plural, one {# edge joins} other {# edges join}} same-coloured nodes. Minimum: {best} colours.

guards.name: Guards
guards.tagline: Watch every road with as few guards as possible.
rules: Click a node to place a guard, click it again to remove it.
A guard watches every road (edge) touching its node: watched roads light up.
Once every road is watched you can submit. You win with the minimum number of guards.
Careful: putting the first guard on the busiest node does not always lead to the best solution.
theory: A set of nodes touching every edge is a vertex cover. Finding a minimum one is among Karp's 21 NP-complete problems (1972): checking a solution is easy, finding one in general is not.

The greedy rule "always take the node with the most unwatched edges" feels natural but can fail, as you have seen. There is a simple trick, though: take any unwatched edge and guard both of its ends. It will not be optimal, but it never uses more than twice the guards needed.

The unguarded nodes form an independent set: no two of them are connected. So minimising guards is the same as maximising the independent set. In bipartite graphs, König's theorem says the minimum cover has the same size as the maximum matching. It is used to place sensors, cameras or network monitors.
guards.lostDetail: You used {used} guards; {best} are enough. The ★ marks show an optimal solution.
